# ARC diagonal ray extension

## Pattern
Some ARC tasks encode a diagonal line with two or more matching-color cells. Extend the line through background-colored cells along its diagonal, preserving every original cell. Continue independently from both endpoints; stop at the grid boundary or before a non-background cell. Do not overwrite obstacles or continue through them.

## Working method
1. Identify the dominant background color.
2. Record all non-background coordinates by color.
3. Find same-color cells lying on a shared diagonal (row and column both change by the same magnitude). Infer the direction from the pair/group.
4. From each endpoint, extend outward along that same diagonal, adding the line color only where the cell is background. Stop before any occupied cell or boundary.
5. Preserve all original markers, including off-line cells; do not infer that an unrelated same-color marker joins the ray unless it lies on the same diagonal.
6. Build and submit the full grid, not just changed coordinates.

## Verified example / key pitfall
In one instance, background was 1. A diagonal pair of 3s at (row 3, col 3) and (row 4, col 2), zero-indexed, extended up-right with 3s at (2,4), (1,5), and (0,6). The opposite ray was blocked by a 4 at (5,1). A pair of 7s at (3,0) and (4,1) had its down-right ray blocked immediately by a 3 at (5,2); do not overwrite it or place 7s beyond it. The 3 at (5,2) was an original off-ray marker and remained unchanged.

Other demonstrations of this task family showed diagonal extensions continuing to the edge when every intervening cell was background. The essential lesson is to honor obstacles: successful extension is not unconditional overwrite-to-edge.

## Caution
A single matching diagonal pair may not determine which of several possible lines is intended if the grid is ambiguous. If demos are available and the cost is acceptable, request one before guessing. Avoid spending submissions on a ray that would have to overwrite a different color.",
